After discarding the poles $x=1$ and $x=-4$, the equation $\dfrac{x+2}{x-1}+\dfrac{2x-3}{x+4}=\dfrac{3x^{2}+5x-2}{(x-1)(x+4)}$ reduces to a linear condition with exactly one surviving real root.
Every real solution of $|x^{2}-6x+5|=3x-4$ is strictly larger than $3$.
Every domain-legal real solution of $\log_{2}(x-1)+\log_{2}(x+3)=\log_{2}(3x+5)$ is strictly larger than $4$.
The equation $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ has at least one negative real solution and at least one real solution greater than $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Begin with the domain of both radicals: $x\ge -1$. Isolate one square root and keep the right-hand side nonnegative:

$$
\sqrt{3x+7}=4-\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
x\le 15
$$

Square once:

$$
3x+7=16-8\sqrt{x+1}+(x+1)
$$

$$
2x-10=-8\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
5-x=4\sqrt{x+1}
$$

which forces the additional restriction $x\le 5$. Square again:

$$
(5-x)^{2}=16(x+1)
$$

$$
x^{2}-26x+9=0
$$

$$
x=13\pm 4\sqrt{10}
$$

Two real candidates appear, but only the smaller one lies in $[-1,5]$ and survives back-substitution. The larger candidate is discarded. So it is not true that both candidates survive.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Work on the common domain that excludes the poles $x=1$ and $x=-4$. Clear the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$:

$$
(x+2)(x+4)+(2x-3)(x-1)=3x^{2}+5x-2
$$

$$
x^{2}+6x+8+2x^{2}-5x+3=3x^{2}+5x-2
$$

$$
3x^{2}+x+11=3x^{2}+5x-2
$$

The quadratic terms cancel, leaving the linear condition

$$
x+11=5x-2
$$

$$
4x=13
$$

$$
x=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

The value $\tfrac{13}{4}$ is neither pole, so exactly one root survives.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An absolute value equals a real expression only when that expression is nonnegative, so require $3x-4\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$. Opening the two sign cases for the quadratic $x^{2}-6x+5$ yields the surviving roots

$$
x=\dfrac{9+3\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx 7.85
$$

and

$$
x=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx 2.62
$$

The second root is real and domain-legal, yet

$$
2.62<3
$$

so it is not true that every real solution is strictly larger than $3$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Logarithms force a strict domain $x>1$ (and $3x+5>0$, which is automatic once $x>1$). Combine the logs into a single product identity:

$$
(x-1)(x+3)=3x+5
$$

$$
x^{2}-x-8=0
$$

$$
x=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}
$$

Only the plus branch is domain-legal:

$$
\dfrac{1+\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 3.37
$$

$$
3.37<4
$$

The unique domain-legal solution is therefore not larger than $4$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Split the absolute value at the kink $x=1$. For $x\ge 1$ the equation becomes $\sqrt{x+3}=5-x$ with the extra restriction $x\le 5$, and squaring yields the admissible root

$$
x=\dfrac{11-\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 2.63>2
$$

For $-3\le x<1$ one obtains $\sqrt{x+3}=3+x$, and squaring yields the two roots $x=-3$ and $x=-2$, both negative and both valid under back-substitution. So there is at least one negative solution and at least one solution greater than $2$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Five independent mixed equations. Work each letter from its own domain restrictions; none of the five collapses by a one-line sum/product identity.

**Part A.** Isolate one radical in $\sqrt{3x+7}+\sqrt{x+1}=4$, square twice, and keep only candidates inside $[-1,5]$ that survive back-substitution — one of the two real roots fails.

**Part B.** Clear the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$ in the rational identity; the quadratic terms cancel and a single linear equation yields $x=\tfrac{13}{4}$, which is not a pole.

**Part C.** Absolute-value cases for $|x^{2}-6x+5|=3x-4$ under $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$ produce two survivors, one of which lies below $3$.

**Part D.** Combine the logs on domain $x>1$ into a quadratic; only $(1+\sqrt{33})/2\approx 3.37$ survives, and that value is less than $4$.

**Part E.** Split $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ at the kink $x=1$; the left piece yields negative roots and the right piece yields a root larger than $2$.

math.title: Print-shop mix — two unknowns, five traps
math.context:
A print shop sells only mono pages and colour pages. In one batch it printed a total of $180$ pages and booked revenue EUR 8100. Mono sells at EUR 35 each and colour at EUR 55 each:
$$
m+c=180,\qquad 35m+55c=8100.
$$
The unique baseline solution is the factual starting point. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The unique baseline solution is $(m,c)=(90,90)$.
If the colour price had been EUR 60 instead of EUR 55, with the same count $m+c=180$ and the same revenue EUR 8100, then $c$ would have fallen below $75$.
If management had printed $15$ fewer mono pages and $15$ more colour pages than the baseline, revenue would have risen by exactly EUR 300.
If total pages stayed $180$ but the revenue target rose to EUR 10000 at the same prices, no nonnegative solution $(m,c)$ would exist, because an all-colour batch only reaches EUR 9900.
If prices stayed EUR 35 and EUR 55 but the shop printed the swapped mix $(120,60)$ instead of the baseline $(90,90)$, revenue would still be EUR 8100.
math.solution_overview:
Two linear equations in the page counts $m$ (mono) and $c$ (colour). Every letter starts from the same baseline solve, then perturbs one coefficient or one mix.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
m+c=180
$$

$$
35m+55c=8100
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

Substitute $m=180-c$ into the revenue equation:

$$
35(180-c)+55c=8100
$$

$$
6300-35c+55c=8100
$$

$$
20c=1800
$$

$$
c=90,\qquad m=90
$$

Baseline mix: $(m,c)=(90,90)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Eliminate $m$ by substituting $m=180-c$ into the revenue equation:

$$
35(180-c)+55c=8100
$$

$$
6300+20c=8100
$$

$$
20c=1800
$$

$$
c=90,\qquad m=90
$$

The unique baseline solution is therefore $(m,c)=(90,90)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Keep the page total $m+c=180$ and the revenue $8100$, but replace the colour price by $60$:

$$
35(180-c)+60c=8100
$$

$$
6300+25c=8100
$$

$$
25c=1800
$$

$$
c=72
$$

Because

$$
72<75
$$

the new colour count falls below $75$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

From the baseline $(90,90)$, shift by $15$ pages:

$$
(m,c)=(75,105)
$$

Revenue at the new mix is

$$
35\cdot 75+55\cdot 105=2625+5775=8400
$$

$$
8400-8100=300
$$

Revenue rises by exactly EUR 300.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

An all-colour batch of $180$ pages yields

$$
55\cdot 180=9900
$$

Any mix that includes mono pages earns strictly less, because mono is cheaper than colour. A target of EUR 10000 therefore exceeds every feasible nonnegative revenue, so no solution $(m,c)$ exists.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Revenue at the swapped mix $(120,60)$ is

$$
35\cdot 120+55\cdot 60=4200+3300=7500
$$

$$
7500\neq 8100
$$

The swapped mix does not preserve the baseline revenue of EUR 8100.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Hard mixed inequalities — varied interval claims
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. All five letters are inequalities, but the claims are worded differently on purpose: absence of counterexamples, existence inside an open interval, existence on a closed interval, containment of a segment, and nonempty intersection.
statements: No point of the interval $[1,4]$ violates $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|\le x+6$.
The inequality $\sqrt{2x+5}+|x-2|\le 4$ admits at least one solution in the open interval $(1,2)$.
There exists some $x\in[0,1]$ for which $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}\ge 1$.
The solution set of $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2$ contains every point of $[0,1]$.
The inequality $\dfrac{|2x-5|}{|x+1|}+|x-2|\le 4$ has nonempty intersection with the interval $[-4,-2]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The claim is a universal “no counterexample” statement on the closed interval $[1,4]$. Critical points of the absolute expressions are $x=1$, $x=4$ and $x=\tfrac{3}{2}$. On $[1,\tfrac{3}{2}]$ the inequality becomes

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(3-2x)\le x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-2x+7
$$

which holds identically (discriminant $4-28<0$). On $\bigl[\tfrac{3}{2},4\bigr]$ it becomes

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(2x-3)\le x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-6x+13
$$

which likewise holds identically (discriminant $36-52<0$). Hence no point of $[1,4]$ is a counterexample.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The claim only asks for existence inside the open interval $(1,2)$. Domain of the radical requires $x\ge -\tfrac{5}{2}$, which already contains $(1,2)$. Isolating cases at the kink $x=2$ and squaring where needed shows that equality can hold inside $(1,2)$, but a direct check at the convenient interior test point $x=\tfrac{3}{2}$ is enough for existence:

$$
\sqrt{3+5}+\left|\tfrac{3}{2}-2\right|=\sqrt{8}+\tfrac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}
$$

$$
2\sqrt{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\approx 2.828+0.5=3.328\le 4
$$

So at least one point of $(1,2)$ satisfies the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Ask whether any point of the closed interval $[0,1]$ can satisfy the rational inequality. Poles are $x=-1$ and $x=2$. For every other $x$,

$$
\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}-1=\dfrac{-4(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+1)}=\dfrac{-4}{x+1}
$$

so the inequality reduces to $x<-1$. The interval $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line. In particular at $x=0$:

$$
\dfrac{6}{-2}=-3\ngeq  1
$$

No point of $[0,1]$ works.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The claim asks for containment of the whole segment $[0,1]$ in the solution set. On $[0,1]$ one has $x\ge 0$, so $|x|=x$, and both $x+3>0$ and $x+1\ge 0$. The inequality reads

$$
\dfrac{x}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2
$$

Each summand is increasing on $[0,1]$, so the left-hand side is maximized at the right endpoint $x=1$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}+\sqrt{2}=0.25+\sqrt{2}\approx 1.664\le 2
$$

At the left endpoint $x=0$:

$$
0+\sqrt{1}=1\le 2
$$

Because the maximum on the segment is already $\le 2$, every point of $[0,1]$ belongs to the solution set.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The claim asks whether the solution set meets $[-4,-2]$. The pole $x=-1$ does not meet that interval, so every point of $[-4,-2]$ is domain-legal. Test the convenient interior point $x=-3$:

$$
\dfrac{|-6-5|}{|-3+1|}+|-3-2|=\dfrac{11}{2}+5=10.5
$$

$$
10.5\le 4
$$

is false. The same failure pattern persists throughout $[-4,-2]$ (the expression stays larger than $4$ on that segment). The intersection with $[-4,-2]$ is therefore empty.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Five mixed inequalities with deliberately varied claim styles: no-counterexample, existence in an open interval, existence on a closed interval, segment containment, and nonempty intersection.

**Part A.** On $[1,4]$ the critical points are $1$, $\tfrac{3}{2}$ and $4$; each piece reduces to a quadratic with negative discriminant that is always nonnegative, so no counterexample exists.

**Part B.** Domain $x\ge -\tfrac{5}{2}$; a direct interior check at $x=\tfrac{3}{2}\in(1,2)$ already witnesses existence.

**Part C.** Cancel the common factor $x-2$ away from the poles to obtain $-4/(x+1)\ge 0$, i.e. $x<-1$; the segment $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line.

**Part D.** On $[0,1]$ the left-hand side is increasing and its maximum at $x=1$ is still $\le 2$, so the whole segment is contained.

**Part E.** Interior testing on $[-4,-2]$ (for instance at $x=-3$) yields values larger than $4$, and the same gap persists across the segment.

math.title: Parametric quadratic family — critical cases
math.context:
For each real parameter $k$, define
$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4).
$$
Decide whether each claim about this family is true or false.
statements: For every real $k$, the equation $g_k(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
The axis of symmetry of $y=g_k(x)$ is $x=k+\tfrac12$ for every $k$.
If $k=2$, then the roots are $x=1$ and $x=5$.
There exists a real $k$ for which both roots are equal to $0$.
The vertex $y$-coordinate equals $-\dfrac{17}{4}$ when $k=0$.
math.solution_overview:
A one-parameter quadratic family. Read the axis, discriminant, and vertex from the coefficients; then specialise $k$ only when a letter asks for it.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4)
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

Axis of symmetry:

$$
x=\frac{2k+1}{2}=k+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Discriminant:

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)=4k+17
$$

Vertex $y$-value at that axis:

$$
g_k\Bigl(k+\tfrac12\Bigr)=-\frac{\Delta}{4}
$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Two distinct real roots require a strictly positive discriminant. Expand

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)=4k^{2}+4k+1-4k^{2}+16=4k+17
$$

At $k=-5$,

$$
\Delta=4(-5)+17=-3<0
$$

so $g_{-5}$ has no real roots. The claim that every real $k$ yields two distinct real roots fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

For a monic quadratic $x^{2}-Bx+C$, the axis is $x=B/2$. Here $B=2k+1$, so

$$
x=\frac{2k+1}{2}=k+\frac{1}{2}
$$

for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Substitute $k=2$:

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-(4+1)x+(4-4)=x^{2}-5x
$$

$$
g_2(x)=x(x-5)
$$

The roots are $0$ and $5$, not $1$ and $5$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A double root at $0$ would require both $g_k(0)=0$ and $g_k'(0)=0$:

$$
g_k(0)=k^{2}-4=0
$$

$$
g_k'(x)=2x-(2k+1)\implies g_k'(0)=-(2k+1)=0
$$

The second forces $k=-\tfrac12$, but then

$$
k^{2}-4=\tfrac14-4=-\tfrac{15}{4}\neq 0
$$

The two conditions are incompatible, so no such $k$ exists.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

For $k=0$ the quadratic is

$$
g_0(x)=x^{2}-x-4
$$

The axis is $x=\tfrac12$, and

$$
g_0\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)=\tfrac14-\tfrac12-4=-\tfrac{17}{4}
$$

which matches the claimed vertex $y$-coordinate.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Courier tariff — affine day/night word problem
math.context: A courier charges a daytime base fee of EUR 12 plus EUR 0.8 per kilometre. Night runs use the same kilometre rate but add a flat night surcharge of EUR 5. Let $d>0$ be the distance in kilometres. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The daytime bill for distance $d$ is exactly $12+0.8d$ euros.
If the same distance were run at night, the night bill would be exactly EUR 5 more than the daytime bill for every $d>0$.
There is a distance $d^{*}$ at which a daytime run and a night run would cost the same; solving $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ finds it.
If the firm waived the EUR 12 base on daytime runs only (charging pure $0.8d$), then for a $20$ km daytime job the client would save exactly EUR 12 compared with the original daytime tariff.
If distance doubled from $10$ km to $20$ km on a daytime run, the bill would also double, because both the base and the kilometre charge scale linearly with $d$.
math.solution_overview:
Day and night tariffs are affine in distance $d>0$. Night adds a constant surcharge, so the two graphs are parallel.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)+5=17+0.8d
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

Same slope $0.8$ and a vertical gap of $5$ imply the graphs never meet: the break-even display

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5
$$

collapses to $0=5$. Waiving the day base at $d=20$ saves exactly $12$ ($28\to 16$). Doubling distance from $10$ to $20$ multiplies the day bill by $28/20=1.4$, not by $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The daytime tariff is a fixed base of $12$ euros plus $0.8$ euros per kilometre:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

which is exactly the claimed daytime bill.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Night runs keep the same kilometre rate and add a flat surcharge of $5$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)+5
$$

for every $d>0$. The night bill is therefore exactly EUR 5 more than the day bill at the same distance.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Set the two bills equal and simplify:

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
0=5
$$

The identity $0=5$ is absurd, so no real break-even distance $d^{*}$ exists. Parallel affine tariffs with a positive gap never meet.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Original daytime bill at $d=20$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+0.8\cdot 20=12+16=28
$$

Waiving the base leaves only the kilometre charge:

$$
0.8\cdot 20=16
$$

$$
28-16=12
$$

The saving is exactly the waived EUR 12 base fee.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Evaluate the daytime bill at the two distances:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+0.8\cdot 10=12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+0.8\cdot 20=12+16=28
$$

Form the ratio:

$$
\frac{C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)}{C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)}=\frac{28}{20}=1.4
$$

$$
1.4\neq 2
$$

Doubling distance multiplies the bill by $1.4$, not by $2$. The kilometre part scales ($8\to 16$), but the fixed base of $12$ does not. Homogeneity would require $C_{\mathrm{day}}(2d)=2\,C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)$; at $d=10$ that would need $28=40$, which fails.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Cubic over quadratic — limits and roots
math.context:
Let
$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0,
$$
be a real cubic, and define
$$
s(x)=\dfrac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}.
$$
Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}s(x)=+\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$, so $x=2$ is at least a double root.
For every choice of $a,b,c,d$ with $a\neq 0$, the horizontal line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $s$.
If $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$, then $r(x)=3x^{2}(x-2)$, so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=2$ is a simple root.
math.solution_overview:
A real cubic $r$ sits over the always-positive quadratic $x^{2}+4$. Asymptotics of $s=r/(x^{2}+4)$ follow from degree, while multiple roots of $r$ follow from shared zeros with $r'$.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0
$$

$$
s(x)=\frac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

Divide through by the leading $x^{2}$ terms:

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

so $s(x)\sim ax$ as $|x|\to\infty$. In particular $\deg r=3>2$ rules out any horizontal asymptote. A shared zero of $r$ and $r'$ at $x=2$ forces multiplicity at least two.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Rewrite the rational function by factoring $ax$ out of the numerator:

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

As $x\to+\infty$ the fraction tends to $1$, so

$$
s(x)\sim ax
$$

When $a>0$ this tends to $+\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A cubic with positive leading coefficient tends to $-\infty$ on the far left:

$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=-\infty\qquad(a>0)
$$

because the $ax^{3}$ term dominates and $x^{3}\to-\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

If a polynomial and its derivative both vanish at the same point, that point is a root of multiplicity at least two. With $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, the factorisation theorem gives

$$
(x-2)^{2}\mid r(x)
$$

so $x=2$ is at least a double root.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Because $\deg r=3>2=\deg(x^{2}+4)$, the asymptotic from Part 2 yields

$$
|s(x)|\to\infty\quad\text{as }|x|\to\infty
$$

The horizontal line $y=0$ is therefore not an asymptote of $s$, for any choice of coefficients with $a\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Substitute the given coefficients:

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{2}(x-2)
$$

The factor $x^{2}$ makes $x=0$ a double root, and the remaining linear factor $x-2$ makes $x=2$ a simple root.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Entangled exponential–log pair — hard compare
math.context:
Define the entangled pair
$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t},\qquad g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}),
$$
and the log-gap
$$
h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)=\ln\!\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr).
$$
Also write $p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $f(t)=g(t)$ has the unique real solution $t=\dfrac{1}{0.9}\ln 4=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$.
$h(t)=\ln 4+0.9t$ for every real $t$, so $h$ is affine with positive slope $0.9$.
If $t$ increases by $\dfrac{10}{3}$, then $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.
The product $p(t)=f(t)g(t)$ is minimized over $\mathbb{R}$ at the same $t$ where $f=g$, and that minimum value equals $64$.
Because $f(0)=4<16=g(0)$ and $f$ grows while $g$ decays, one has $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.
math.solution_overview:
Two exponential trajectories and the log-gap between them. Every letter follows from the three closed forms below.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t},\qquad g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr),\qquad p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{4}{16}e^{0.9t}=\tfrac14 e^{0.9t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\tfrac14+0.9t=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

$$
p(t)=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

Crossing $f=g$ solves $e^{0.9t}=4$, so $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set the two trajectories equal and collect the exponential:

$$
4e^{0.3t}=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
e^{0.9t}=4
$$

$$
t=\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}
$$

Uniqueness follows because $t\mapsto e^{0.9t}$ is one-to-one on $\mathbb{R}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Expand the log-gap from Part 2:

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{4e^{0.3t}}{16e^{-0.6t}}\Bigr)=\ln\Bigl(\tfrac14 e^{0.9t}\Bigr)
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\tfrac14+0.9t=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

The constant term is $-\ln 4$, not $+\ln 4$. The claimed formula $\ln 4+0.9t$ is therefore wrong (though the slope $0.9$ is correct).

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Shift the argument by $\tfrac{10}{3}$ and factor the extra exponential:

$$
f\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=4e^{0.3t+1}=e\cdot f(t)
$$

$$
g\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=16e^{-0.6t-2}=e^{-2}g(t)
$$

because $0.3\cdot\tfrac{10}{3}=1$ and $-0.6\cdot\tfrac{10}{3}=-2$. So $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ by $e^{-2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The product simplifies to a pure exponential:

$$
p(t)=4e^{0.3t}\cdot 16e^{-0.6t}=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

Because the exponent $-0.3t$ is strictly decreasing in $t$, $p$ has no global minimum on $\mathbb{R}$. At the crossing $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$ one gets

$$
p\Bigl(\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}\Bigr)=64e^{-0.3\cdot(\ln 4)/0.9}\neq 64
$$

in general. Both halves of the claim fail.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At $t=0$ one does have $f(0)=4<16=g(0)$, and $f$ grows while $g$ decays. But they meet at the positive crossing

$$
t^{*}=\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}>0
$$

where $f(t^{*})=g(t^{*})$, and for all $t>t^{*}$ one has $f(t)>g(t)$. The claim that $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$ is therefore false.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Tangled revenue path — marginal analysis
math.context: A firm faces inverse demand $P(q)=90-3q$ for $0\le q\le 30$ (price in euros, quantity in thousands of units). Revenue is $R(q)=q\cdot P(q)$. Marginal revenue means $R'(q)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $R'(q)=90-6q$, so in particular $R'(4)=66$.
Revenue is maximised at the same quantity where $P(q)=0$, i.e. at the choke quantity $q=30$.
If output rises from $q=4$ to $q=5$, the linear approximation using $R'(4)$ overestimates the true revenue increase $R(5)-R(4)$, because $R$ is a concave quadratic.
At the quantity that maximises $R$, price equals marginal revenue.
Cutting price enough to raise quantity from $q=16$ to $q=17$ must raise revenue, because more units are sold.
math.solution_overview:
Linear inverse demand produces a concave quadratic revenue path. Marginal revenue is the derivative; the revenue peak is where that derivative vanishes.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
P(q)=90-3q,\qquad 0\le q\le 30
$$

$$
R(q)=q\cdot P(q)=90q-3q^{2}
$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

$$
R'(q)=90-6q,\qquad R''(q)=-6<0
$$

Revenue is maximised at

$$
R'(q)=0\implies q=15
$$

where $P(15)=45\neq 0$ and $R'(15)=0$. Past $q=15$, marginal revenue is negative.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand revenue and differentiate:

$$
R(q)=q(90-3q)=90q-3q^{2}
$$

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

$$
R'(4)=90-24=66
$$

which matches the claimed marginal revenue at $q=4$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Maximise $R$ by setting marginal revenue to zero:

$$
90-6q=0
$$

$$
q=15
$$

Choke price $P(q)=0$ forces $q=30$, where $R(30)=0$. The revenue-maximising quantity $15$ is not the choke quantity $30$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The true increment from $q=4$ to $q=5$ is

$$
R(5)-R(4)=(90\cdot 5-3\cdot 25)-(90\cdot 4-3\cdot 16)=375-312=63
$$

The linear approximation using $R'(4)$ predicts

$$
R'(4)\cdot 1=66
$$

Because $R''(q)=-6<0$, the graph is concave and the tangent overestimates the increment: $66>63$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At the revenue-maximising quantity $q=15$,

$$
R'(15)=0
$$

while price is still positive:

$$
P(15)=90-3\cdot 15=45\neq 0
$$

Price does not equal marginal revenue at the revenue peak (that equality would require $P(q)=0$, which is the choke point, not the peak).

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Past the revenue peak $q=15$, marginal revenue is already negative:

$$
R'(16)=90-96=-6<0
$$

Moving from $q=16$ to $q=17$ therefore lowers revenue even though more units are sold. Selling more does not raise revenue on the declining side of $R$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
math.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result is greater than 7%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result is greater than 3.4%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result is greater than 45%.
The probability that a tested deer receives a negative result equals 1 minus the probability that a tested deer receives a positive result.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result is greater than the probability that the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compute the unconditional positive-test probability from first principles. For each subspecies, mix true positives and false positives with the subspecies-specific prevalence:

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_A)=(0.90)(0.02)+(0.04)(0.98)=0.0572
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_B)=(0.90)(0.06)+(0.04)(0.94)=0.0916
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_C)=(0.90)(0.15)+(0.04)(0.85)=0.169
$$

Average over the subspecies priors by the law of total probability:

$$
P(T^{+})=(0.0572)(0.60)+(0.0916)(0.25)+(0.169)(0.15)
$$

$$
P(T^{+})=0.03432+0.0229+0.02535=0.08257
$$

Compare with the claimed threshold $7\%=0.07$:

$$
0.08257>0.07
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The joint event “Subspecies A and a positive test” factors through the conditional positive rate already computed for A:

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_A)=(0.90)(0.02)+(0.04)(0.98)=0.0572
$$

$$
P(S_A)=0.60
$$

$$
P(S_A\cap T^{+})=P(T^{+}\mid S_A)P(S_A)=(0.0572)(0.60)=0.03432
$$

Compare with $3.4\%=0.034$:

$$
0.03432>0.034
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Apply Bayes’ theorem to the posterior subspecies probability given a positive test. First recover the joint and the marginal:

$$
P(S_A\cap T^{+})=(0.0572)(0.60)=0.03432
$$

$$
P(T^{+})=0.03432+0.0229+0.02535=0.08257
$$

$$
P(S_A\mid T^{+})=\frac{P(S_A\cap T^{+})}{P(T^{+})}=\frac{0.03432}{0.08257}\approx 0.4156=41.56\%
$$

The claim needs more than $45\%$. Because $41.56\%$ is not greater than $45\%$, the claim fails.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A field test returns either a positive or a negative result; those two outcomes partition the sample space. Formally, $T^{-}$ is the complement of $T^{+}$:

$$
T^{-}=(T^{+})^{c}
$$

Probability of the complement is therefore one minus the positive-test probability:

$$
P(T^{-})=1-P(T^{+})
$$

No independence or prevalence assumption is required — the identity follows from complementarity alone. With the recovered value $P(T^{+})=0.08257$ one could also write $P(T^{-})=0.91743$, but the equality itself is what the claim asserts.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Compare the two posterior subspecies probabilities given a positive test. Form each joint probability first:

$$
P(S_C\cap T^{+})=P(T^{+}\mid S_C)P(S_C)=(0.169)(0.15)=0.02535
$$

$$
P(S_B\cap T^{+})=P(T^{+}\mid S_B)P(S_B)=(0.0916)(0.25)=0.0229
$$

Divide by the same marginal $P(T^{+})=0.08257$:

$$
P(S_C\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.02535}{0.08257}\approx 0.3069
$$

$$
P(S_B\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.0229}{0.08257}\approx 0.2773
$$

Compare the two posteriors:

$$
0.3069>0.2773
$$

so $P(S_C\mid T^{+})>P(S_B\mid T^{+})$. Equivalently, because both posteriors share the same denominator $P(T^{+})$, it is enough to compare the joints $0.02535>0.0229$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
This problem describes a population of deer composed of three subspecies, each with a different prevalence of a certain prion disease. A field test for the disease has a known sensitivity and false-positive rate. We are testing a randomly selected deer and observing a positive result.

Let $S_A$, $S_B$, and $S_C$ be the events that a randomly selected deer belongs to Subspecies A, B, or C, respectively. Their prior probabilities are:
$$P(S_A) = 0.60$$
$$P(S_B) = 0.25$$
$$P(S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $D$ be the event that a deer has the prion disease. The prevalence rates for each subspecies are:
$$P(D \mid S_A) = 0.02$$
$$P(D \mid S_B) = 0.06$$
$$P(D \mid S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $T^+$ be the event of a positive test result and $T^-$ be the event of a negative test result. The test characteristics are:
Sensitivity: $P(T^+ \mid D) = 0.90$
False-positive rate: $P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 0.04$

This means:
$P(T^- \mid D) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10$
$P(T^- \mid D^c) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 1 - 0.04 = 0.96$

To evaluate the probabilities involving test results, we first need to find the probability of a positive test result for a deer from each subspecies, considering its specific disease prevalence. This uses the Law of Total Probability for each subspecies:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) P(D^c \mid S_i)$$
Since the test characteristics are independent of subspecies, $P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D)$ and $P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D^c)$.
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c) (1 - P(D \mid S_i))$$

For Subspecies A:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(1 - 0.02)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(0.98)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_A) = 0.018 + 0.0392 = 0.0572
$$

For Subspecies B:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(1 - 0.06)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(0.94)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_B) = 0.054 + 0.0376 = 0.0916
$$

For Subspecies C:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(1 - 0.15)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(0.85)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_C) = 0.135 + 0.034 = 0.169
$$

Now, to find the overall probability that a randomly tested deer receives a positive result, we use the Law of Total Probability over the subspecies:
$$P(T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_A)P(S_A) + P(T^+ \mid S_B)P(S_B) + P(T^+ \mid S_C)P(S_C)$$
$$P(T^+) = (0.0572)(0.60) + (0.0916)(0.25) + (0.169)(0.15)$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.03432 + 0.0229 + 0.02535$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.08257$$
This is the base probability for many subsequent calculations.

math.title: Harbor Foghorn Tests
math.context: Harbor staff run 14 independent foghorn tests. The expected number of clear audible tests is 11.2. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The next test fails with probability 0.2.
The expected number of audible tests in the next 12 tests is 4.8.
The variance of the number of audible tests out of 50 tests is 8.
The probability of 3 consecutive audible tests is less than 0.3.
The probability of at most 4 audible tests in the next 6 tests is more than 0.5.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From the stem quantities, recover the common success probability step by step.

$$
p = \dfrac{E[X]}{n} = \dfrac{11.2}{14} = 0.8
$$

Each independent trial either succeeds or fails, so the failure probability is the complement

$$
1-p
$$

Substituting the recovered value,

$$
1-p = 1-0.8
$$

$$
1 - 0.8 = 0.2
$$

This agrees with the probability stated in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

For a binomial count $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the mean is the product of the number of trials and the success probability:

$$
E[X] = np
$$

math.solution_overview:
Harbor staff run independent foghorn tests whose clear-audible outcomes form a binomial count. The stem supplies the mean over a block of $14$ trials; every letter reuses the recovered success probability.

**Part 1: Setup.**

Let $X$ be the number of clear audible tests in $n$ independent trials with common success probability $p$. Model

$$
X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)
$$

The stem gives $n=14$ and $E[X]=11.2$. Failures occur with probability $1-p$, and the variance identity is $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.

**Part 2: Solve.**

Recover $p$ from the mean formula $E[X]=np$:

$$
p=\dfrac{E[X]}{n}=\dfrac{11.2}{14}=0.8
$$

Hence $1-p=0.2$. Subsequent letters only change the trial count $n$ (or ask for a short independent run of successes) while keeping this same $p$.
